content_html_sanitized:
WASHINGTON, Dec. 30  As new data showing "drug-related" hospital emergencies are on the decline for the first time in six years, HHS Secretary Donna Shalala misused the numbers to continue to lie to the American   people about marijuana.  What both the Associated Press and UPI misreported as "the growing number of marijuana cases -- more than 50,000 in 1996" Shalala said ``provides a loud and clear message that marijuana is a powerful drug with potentially serious consequences.''  

Now for the facts:

The numbers in question, the semiannual Drug Abuse Warning Network (DAWN) study show hospital emergency rooms treated 487,600 people for self-reported problems related of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamines and other drugs in 1996, down 6 percent from 1995. The study has collected annual and semiannual data on drug-related emergencies from a representative sample of U.S. hospitals since the 1970s. The decrease is largely attributable to fewer cases involving legal drugs. There were significant drops in cases involving pain relievers aspirin, ibuprofen and acetaminophen.  (See Deadly Drug Sold by Founder of Partnership for A Drug-Free America, Says Forbes) Also falling were the number of cases involving methamphetamine, or speed, and PCP.

Half the cases were drug overdoses, and another 37 percent were attempted suicides, the report said. (Note: there is no lethal dose of marijuana.) The most common cases were alcohol used in combination with another drug; there were nearly 160,000 of these cases last year, down slightly from 168,000 in 1995. Cocaine and heroin were the next most common cases, at 144,180 and 70,463, respectively, both essentially unchanged from 1995.

Note: one visit to the emergency room often involves more than one drug, so the individual statistics add up to more than the total number of visits.

These numbers involve emergency room "mentions" of all the drugs cited by patients. People entering emergency rooms are necessarily asked about what "drugs" they have been using. That would make a significant difference in how they are medicated. Thus, if a person having trouble with heroin or cocaine or alcohol mentions that they were also using marijuana -- even to ease the pain of withdrawal -- this is recorded in these numbers. For those cases involving only mentions of marijuana, cannabis still may not have been the cause of their visit. For those cases in which marijuana was the cause of the visit -- only a tiny fraction of one percent of all ER visits -- almost all involve nothing more serious than transitory panic attacks. In other words, these numbers are not necessarily about the cause of the visit, nor do they reflect on the seriousness of the problems experienced.

Donna Shalala should know this. Consequently, she is either so incompetent that she does not know anything about health care statistics, or she is so indifferent to the truth that she is ideally suited to be a prohibitionist propagandist, which is all that she is. It is truly appalling that someone whose job it is to advance to the health of the American people would use the position to just the opposite and lie to justify the continuing arrest  of the sick, dying and disabled, and the suppression of a plant that would alleviate the suffering of so many others.

Someone had to say this, and I just did.
